result.summary: The Greeks, guided by Calchas and Ulysses' plan, build the Wooden Horse with Athena's help, while the gods clash until Zeus stops them. The chiefs hide in the Horse, Sinon deceives the Trojans, Laocoon is punished, and the Horse is dragged into Troy despite Cassandra's warnings.

scenes.title: Council of the Greek chiefs
scenes.summary: Calchas reads an omen and Ulysses proposes the Horse stratagem. Neoptolemus and Philoctetes resist until Zeus's thunder makes them yield.
scenes.stakes: The Greeks risk endless failed siege; Neoptolemus and Philoctetes risk Zeus's wrath.

scenes.title: Epeius builds the Horse
scenes.summary: Athena appears in a dream to Epeius, and the Greeks fell timber on Ida and build the Horse in three days.

scenes.title: War of the gods
scenes.summary: While Zeus is away the gods fight by the Xanthus until he returns in wrath and Themis persuades them to stop.
scenes.stakes: The gods risk being buried under mountains by Zeus.

scenes.title: The chiefs enter the Horse
scenes.summary: Ulysses urges the ambush, Sinon volunteers, Nestor is refused entry, and the chiefs climb in. The rest burn the tents and sail to Tenedos.
scenes.stakes: The hidden warriors risk death if the plan is discovered.

scenes.title: Sinon and Laocoon
scenes.summary: Trojans torture Sinon, who tells his false tale. Athena blinds Laocoon and the Trojans drag the Horse into Troy.
scenes.stakes: Sinon risks torture and death; Troy risks ruin.

scenes.title: Serpents and omens
scenes.summary: Athena sends serpents that kill Laocoon's sons, and dire portents follow the Trojans' sacrifices.
scenes.stakes: Laocoon and his sons face death; Troy faces divine doom.

scenes.title: Cassandra's warning
scenes.summary: Cassandra prophesies ruin and tries to burn the Horse, but the Trojans stop her and go on feasting.
scenes.stakes: Cassandra risks scorn; Troy faces destruction.

alias_notes.explanation: Greek form of the name, used once in this translation.

notable_quotes.reason: Nestor's reflection that the path to ruin is easy and the path to fame hard.
Captures Cassandra's curse: true prophecy never believed.

analysis.text: Cunning triumphs over force, and mortals are shown as playthings of divine will and fate.
This is the Posthomeric epic of Quintus of Smyrna, filling in events after the Iliad, drawing on older lost epics.

legacy.text: The Trojan Horse became a proverb for deceptive gifts and a computer 'Trojan' malware name.

fun_facts.text: Quintus says he first received inspiration while tending sheep near Smyrna.

language_notes.text: Danaan: Greek. The Greeks are also called Argives and Achaeans in this translation.
Hests means commands or bidding; here, the divine promptings that inspire Calchas's prophecy.
Leaguer means siege; the Greeks have been besieging Troy's walls.
Laertes' son is Ulysses, identified by his father's name. Burg means fortified town.
Pallas's image is the Palladium, a sacred statue of Athena stolen from Troy. Ulysses's lie claims the Horse atones for this theft.
Rede means counsel or advice. Odysseus is the Greek form of Ulysses, here used by Calchas.
Nidderings is an archaic word for cowards or wretches.
Aeacus' son is Achilles; the speaker calls Neoptolemus his child. Achilles died before Troy fell.
Epeius is the Greek craftsman who built the Horse. Athena was the goddess of crafts, so she taught him.
"What time" is archaic for "at the time when"; the sentence dates the hour as deep night, when the stars have wheeled across the sky.
Erebus is the dark region of the underworld; here night is imagined as being driven back down into it by the dawn.
The Argives, Achaeans and Danaans are all names for the Greeks; Argos stands for the Greek host generally.
"Bare" is the archaic past tense of "bear"; the Greeks carried the timber down. "Shagged" means rough with thick growth.
"Hest" in the preceding sentence means command; here "unsawn" shows the trunks were not yet cut into planks.
Pallas is another name for Athena, used here for the goddess who decrees the work.
Epeius built the Wooden Horse; 'Epeius' work' is the Horse by which the Greeks tricked the Trojans.
Danaans: a name for the Greeks, from Danaus; used interchangeably with Argives and Achaeans.
Ilium is Troy; 'Fair Ilium' refers to the city itself.
'Her high peaks' refers to Ida's own summits, which the gods tear off and throw as missiles.
'Ear' here is a misprint or variant for 'car', meaning chariot; the same applies later in the sentence.
Welkin means the sky or vault of heaven.
'It ill beseems' means it is unbecoming or improper; 'creatures of a day' means short-lived mortals.
"Laertes' son" is a patronymic for Ulysses, who is named here by his father's name rather than his own.
"Emprise" means an adventurous or daring undertaking.
Tritonis is a name for Athena, to whom the Trojans will think the Horse is offered. This translation uses Greek-derived epithets.
The speaker addresses Ulysses as "Odysseus," though the translation usually uses Ulysses elsewhere. It is the same man.
"I trow" means "I believe" or "I am confident."
Nestor recalls the building and sailing of the Argo, Jason's ship (Aeson's son) in the quest for the Golden Fleece. King Pelias sent Jason on that voyage.
"Peril-fain" means eager for danger.
The poet, Quintus of Smyrna, invokes the Muses (Queens of Song) and describes his youth tending sheep near Smyrna.
"Clomb" is an archaic past tense of "climbed."
Hellespont is the strait (now the Dardanelles) beside Troy; here it means the shore where the Greek camp had been.
Danaans are the Greeks, named for the legendary Danaus; Argives and Achaeans are other names for them.
"Shore away" means cut off; "in every wise" means in every way.
"Recked not" means took no heed of; "outrage foul" is the shameful mutilation.
The stolen guardian image is the Palladium, Athena's statue, taken from Troy by Ulysses and Diomedes; Sinon claims the Horse atones for this.
Wine drops and hallowed meal were the usual preparations of a sacrificial victim, so Sinon claims he was ritually readied for death.
"Had 'scaped" means would have escaped; the sentence says Athena's intervention alone prevented this.
"Prey-giver" is an epithet of Athena, as giver of spoils.
Enyo is a Greek war goddess, associated with battle's bloodshed.
"Coronal" means crown; the walls are likened to a crown encircling the city.
Typhon was a monstrous serpent-limbed giant of Greek myth, defeated by Zeus; his brood here means fearsome snake-like creatures.
Xanthus and Simois are the rivers of the Trojan plain; their 'daughters' are river-nymphs. 'Cyprian Queen' is Aphrodite, who favoured Troy.
'Fleers' means those who flee; 'forgat' is an archaic form of 'forgot'.
'Ravined' means devoured greedily; 'sightless sire' refers to Laocoon, who had been blinded.
'Hest' means command; 'fane' means temple; Pallas is another name for Athena.
A cenotaph is an empty tomb built in memory of those whose bodies are not available.
'Portionless' of the sun's light means deprived of sight, that is, blind.
'Dardanus' sons' means the Trojans, descended from Dardanus, the ancestor of Troy's royal line.
Apollo gave Cassandra true prophecy but doomed her never to be believed, after she rejected him; hence her words fall as 'idle wind'.
'Land of Darkness' means the underworld, the realm of the dead, which she says the Trojans are entering.
The Erinyes are the avenging Furies; 'Helen's spousals' refers to Helen's marriage to Paris, the cause of the war.
'Path of Ghosts' is the road to the underworld; the Trojans are close to death.
Laocoon was the priest who warned against the Horse and was killed, with his sons, by sea serpents.
'Fain' means eager or gladly willing.
A halberd is a long-shafted weapon with an axe blade and spike.

context_notes.text: Calchas is the Greek seer who interprets omens. Phoebus is Apollo, god of prophecy.
Tenedos is an island close to Troy where the Greeks hid their fleet while pretending to leave.
Neoptolemus is Achilles' son, and Philoctetes is the archer who holds Hercules' bow. Both joined the war late, so they are eager to fight.
Dardania is a name for the Trojan land, after the ancestor Dardanus.
Athena, goddess of wisdom and craft, favoured the Greeks. She helps plan the Horse, the trick that will bring down Troy.
Epeius was the Greek craftsman who built the Horse. In Homer he is a boxer and carpenter, and Athena is his patron.
The sons of Atreus are Agamemnon and Menelaus, the Greek leaders. Ida is the mountain near Troy, a source of timber.
Ocean and Tethys were Titan deities of the world-encircling river and its waters; Zeus visits the far edge of the world.
Xanthus is the river of Troy, also called Scamander, beside which the Trojan War was fought.
Ares, god of war, sided with Troy; Athena favoured the Greeks, so their clash is natural.
Hades is the underworld; the Titans were older gods imprisoned beneath the earth by Zeus.
Themis is the goddess of divine order and law, hence her authority to restrain the quarrelling gods.
Sinon is the Greek who will let himself be captured by the Trojans and persuade them to take the Horse into the city.
Achilles' son is Neoptolemus, also called Pyrrhus. He joined the war after his father's death.
This catalogue names Greek leaders who hid inside the Horse. Accounts differ on how many entered and who they were.
Epeius built the Horse, so he alone knows how its hidden door opens and closes.
Tenedos is an island near Troy where the Greek fleet hid so the Trojans would think the Greeks had left.
Sinon is a Greek left behind to deceive the Trojans into taking the Horse into the city.
Calchas was the Greek seer who interpreted omens for the army.
Laocoon was a Trojan priest who warned against the Horse.
Epeius was the Greek craftsman who built the Wooden Horse.
Laocoon was a Trojan priest who warned against the wooden horse and offended Athena, who favoured the Greeks.
Phoebus is Apollo, Troy's protector; laurel (bay) trees were sacred to him, so their withering signals his departure.
Cassandra, daughter of King Priam, was a Trojan princess and prophetess.
The Argive (Greek) warriors are hidden inside the wooden Horse, waiting to emerge at night and sack Troy.

literary_notes.text: The falcon and dove story is an omen that works as a fable. The patient hunter stands for the Greeks, the dove for Troy.
The general truth about desperate men is stated as a maxim. It justifies avoiding a direct assault.
Neoptolemus's scorn for walls and trickery shows him as a hot-blooded warrior, like his father, who values open combat.
Zeus's anger is shown through the shaking earth and shuddering air, as nature itself seems to react to his wrath.
Compound descriptions like "splendour-kindled" and "far-flashing" give the epic a Homeric grandeur, here setting the divine scene.
Epeius's craft ideas are pictured as soldiers marching in order through his soul, showing his mind filled with the plan.
The wooden Horse grows like a living creature, stressing the divine help behind human skill.
The wood seems to have spirit and speed and even to neigh, praising the lifelike craftsmanship.
The Horse's coming fame hints at its role in Troy's fall and its place in later tradition.
The cry reaching from heaven to Hades and shaking the Titans magnifies the scale of the gods' battle.
Ridges sigh, streams sob and ravines groan, so the whole landscape seems to mourn the divine conflict.
'Iris rainbow-plumed' uses a descriptive epithet in epic style, as with 'all-contriving Fate' earlier.
Immortals trembling in fear is ironic, showing Zeus's power exceeds that of all the other gods.
Themis's speech presents her as the voice of reason and shows divine hierarchy and the gods' folly in fighting over mortals.
The general truth that a desperate man may overcome a stronger enemy is offered as a persuasive maxim.
"Marked of destiny" hints that Sinon's role will be decisive to the outcome.
The easy path to ruin is set against the hard path to fame, which makes the point about toil and reward.
The narrator directly addresses the Muses, following the epic tradition of invoking them before a catalogue.
"'Twixt victory and death" pictures the men as suspended between two outcomes, which conveys their tension.
The dawn "uprose" on their hopes and fears, as if the day itself arrives to meet their anxiety.
Sinon's body is compared to firm rock, stressing his unyielding endurance under torture.
Sinon's courage and steadfast lie are divinely aided by Hera, who favors Troy's destruction.
Eyes running with fluid are compared to a stream turbid with melting snow, making the pain vivid.
The dragging of the Horse is likened to launching a ship, with groaning rollers adding ominous sound.
The Trojans haul in their own doom, which the narrator and reader know but they do not.
Laocoon's ignored warning points to the coming destruction of Troy.
The serpents' passage is likened to an earthquake, conveying their supernatural power.
Troy becoming 'one shriek' of fleeing people exaggerates the panic into a single collective sound.
The mother is compared to a nightingale whose chicks a serpent killed, ironically echoing the serpents that killed her sons.
Weeping statues, bloody offerings and groaning walls are omens of Troy's coming destruction.
The Trojans ignore the portents and revel, since fate has clouded their minds, making their doom ironic and inevitable.
Her cry is compared to a wounded lioness whose pain makes her fiercer, conveying Cassandra's grief-fueled power.
Her neck writhing like a wind-shaken sapling shows her frenzied, possessed state.
The darkening of 'their last night' signals Troy's imminent fall.
The hidden Greeks marvel at Cassandra's accuracy while the Trojans dismiss her, heightening the tragedy.
Cassandra is likened to a wounded pantheress driven off by hounds yet turning back, showing fierce, defiant anguish.
